CHAPTERS.title: What is intellectual property?
CHAPTERS.summary: Definition of IP, its four aims, the consequence of an IP right, French classification and the five main IP rights with their conditions and duration.
CHAPTERS.html:
1. Definition

Intellectual property is defined by opposition to the ownership of physical goods:

  • Property (literal sense): ownership of something tangible (a car, a house).
  • Intellectual property (IP): ownership of a creation that has no physical form (e.g. a trademark) or is a product of the human mind (software, a book, a poem). It is the product of a person's inventiveness, reflection or creativity.
  • IP law = all the legal rules that allow the recognition and protection of intellectual or intangible creations. It grants the author exclusive rights over the work.
Exclusive right = only the holder may exploit the creation, for a certain period of time and within a defined territory. Example from the slides: a technology that took 10 years to develop is patented so that nobody can copy it and the inventor is rewarded for the investment.

2. The four aims of IP law

  1. Protect creators and innovators by granting an exclusive right to exploit their works or inventions. Any use must be authorised by the creator and compensated.
  2. Promote innovation, creativity and investment: creating takes time and money (some writers take 10 years to write a book), so the law protects creators to encourage them to create.
  3. Provide financial incentives to creators, inventors and entrepreneurs and prevent copying or imitation by competitors. Without IP, competitors could copy cheaply (often with lower quality), which destroys the return on investment.
  4. Guarantee the quality of products and services for consumers: a brand is associated with a standard of quality. A company that owns a trademark has a reputation to protect, so poor quality reduces the value of its brand. The trademark signals that the product comes from the original source (consistency, safety, reliability).

3. Consequence of obtaining an IP right

The owner obtains an exclusive right over the use, reproduction, distribution or commercial exploitation of the work or invention, and can prohibit others from doing the same without authorisation.

Slide example: I launch the clothing brand YBX and register it. The registration protects the brand itself against copying or unauthorised use in the same field. The common designs of the clothes are not protected by the trademark.

IP rights do not apply automatically to every creation. A creation is protected only if it meets the specific criteria of the IP right concerned.

4. The two branches of IP in French law

In France, IP rules are in the Intellectual Property Code (Code de la propriété intellectuelle, CPI). IP is divided into two areas:

Literary and artistic property (propriété littéraire et artistique)Industrial property (propriété industrielle)
Copyright, software, databasesPatents, trademarks, designs

5. The main IP rights (reminder table, slide 47)

RightWhat it protectsConditionsDuration
CopyrightAn original literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, software1. Original work (author's personal touch)
2. Must be expressed (not just an idea)		Author's life + 70 years after death (EU standard)
DesignThe appearance (shape, lines, colours) of a product1. Novelty
2. Individual character		5 years, renewable up to 25 years maximum
PatentTechnical inventions (a product or a process)1. Novelty (not part of the prior art)
2. Inventive step (not obvious to a skilled person)
3. Industrial application		20 years from filing date (annual renewal fees)
TrademarkDistinctive signs (names, logos, slogans)Distinctive (not generic); capable of representation; available (not already registered)10 years, renewable indefinitely
Geographical indication (GI)The name of a product linked to a geographical areaLink between quality/reputation/characteristics and the geographical originUnlimited, as long as the link and specifications are maintained

Another slide lists the patent conditions as: (i) a new invention, (ii) in a technological field, (iii) involving an inventive step, (iv) capable of industrial application.

Design definition in the slides: exclusive right over the fixed and new appearance/shape of a product that has an individual character.

Trademark definition in the slides: a sign (words, names, designs, letters, numerals, colours, the shape of goods, sounds…) capable of (1) distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings and (2) being represented on the register.

6. Geographical indications (slide 46)

LabelMeaningExample
PDO (AOP) / AOCProtected designation of origin: the principal production steps follow a well-established technique within the same geographical area, which gives the product its characteristics. European symbol protecting the name throughout the EU. The AOC refers to products meeting the PDO criteria and protects the name on the French territory.Champagne
PGI (IGP)Protected geographical indication: an agricultural product, raw or processed, whose quality, reputation or other characteristics are linked to its geographical origin. Applies to agricultural, agro-food and wine sectors.Bayonne ham
IG for industrial and hand-crafted products (FR, since 2014)Name of a place used to designate a product other than agricultural, forestry, food or sea products, which originates there and has a quality, reputation or characteristics mainly attributable to that origin.Limoges porcelain
  • Saying a trademark lasts 20 years (that is the patent). Trademark = 10 years, renewable indefinitely.
  • Putting trademarks in "literary and artistic property". Trademarks are industrial property.
  • Forgetting that an IP right is limited in time and in territory.

CHAPTERS.title: Other protected distinctive signs
CHAPTERS.summary: Registered company name, commercial name and domain name: how they differ from a trademark, how they are protected (tort / unfair competition) and the principle of specialty.
CHAPTERS.html:
Besides the trademark, three other distinctive signs are protected:

  1. the registered name of a company (dénomination sociale)
  2. the commercial name (nom commercial)
  3. the domain name (nom de domaine)
These signs (1) have no common legislation and (2) can only be protected through a lawsuit for tortious liability (responsabilité délictuelle), more precisely for unfair competition (concurrence déloyale). This is not an IP infringement action (≠ contrefaçon).

1. Registered name of a company

The name under which a company is registered: the name of the legal person (personne morale). Trademark ≠ registered name.

The company can act against any use in France of:

  1. an identical or similar sign,
  2. for an identical or similar activity,
  3. that is likely to create confusion in the consumer's mind.

Sanction: lawsuit in tort for unfair competition.

2. Commercial name

The name under which a merchant carries on the activity. It can be affixed on the door, on communications, on products. Commercial name ≠ trademark.

Protection against any use: (1) where the name is registered, (2) of an identical or similar sign, (3) for an identical or similar activity, (4) in the same geographical area where the merchant operates, that is likely to create confusion in the consumer's mind.

Sanction: tort, unfair competition.

3. Domain name

The name registered to identify the address of a website (e.g. www.example.fr). Domain name ≠ trademark.

Protection against any use: (1) where the domain name is registered, (2) of an identical or similar sign, (3) for an identical or similar activity, (4) in the same geographical area where the website operates, likely to create confusion in the public's mind.

Sanction: tort, unfair competition.

4. The principle of specialty

All distinctive signs, including trademarks, are limited by the principle of specialty (principe de spécialité): a sign is protected only for the goods and services for which it is used or registered. Example: "Sandro" is only protected for fashion items.

5. Summary table and examples

SignDefinitionExample
TrademarkSign capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from others, and capable of representation (smells and tastes cannot be represented)E.LECLERC, Eco+, Repère, "Nos régions ont du talent"
Registered company nameLegal name of the company as registered with the authoritiesInditex (registered name behind Zara)
Commercial nameName under which a business operates publiclyLECLERC
Domain nameAn internet addresswww.example.com
Geographical indicationIndicates that a product originates from a specific placeChampagne
CompanyRegistered nameTrade/business nameBrand namesDomain

GoogleAlphabet Inc.GoogleGooglegoogle.com

  • Saying that the owner of a company name or domain name sues for infringement (contrefaçon). Without an IP right, the action is tort / unfair competition.
  • Forgetting the geographical limit of a commercial name and domain name.
  • Confusing the group's registered name (Alphabet Inc.) with its brand (Google).

CHAPTERS.title: The trademark: definition and functions
CHAPTERS.summary: Legal definition (Art. 3 Directive 2015/2436), trademark vs. certification and collective marks, and the four functions recognised by the CJEU with the four key cases.
CHAPTERS.html:
1. A trademark is intellectual property

It involves creating new or existing elements to identify goods and services (a creative activity). It is the link that connects the sign to the goods and services. Its first aim: avoid confusion in the eyes of the public by preventing a competitor from using the sign.

2. Trademark ≠ certification mark ≠ collective mark

TypeDefinitionExample in slides
Trademark (individual)Sign distinguishing the goods/services of one undertaking from those of othersE.LECLERC, Eco+, Repère
Certification markSign indicating that goods/services comply with standards set by the owner of the mark: quality, materials, mode of manufacture, accuracy, other characteristicsFairtrade
Collective markSign distinguishing goods/services of the members of an association that owns the mark. Used by several members, it shows membership and often common standards"Vignerons indépendants", Intermarché

Note: one slide labels "Vignerons indépendants" as "Example of certification mark" but it sits under the collective mark definition; read it as a collective mark.

3. The legal definition

Art. 3 Directive (EU) 2015/2436:

"A trademark may consist of any signs, in particular words, including personal names, or designs, letters, numerals, colours, the shape of goods or of the packaging of goods, or sounds, provided that such signs are capable of: (a) distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings; and (b) being represented on the register in a manner which enables the competent authorities and the public to determine the clear and precise subject matter of the protection afforded to its proprietor."
Two criteria to register a trademark: distinctiveness + capacity of representation. To be protected, the mark must be registered with the competent public authority and clearly described so everyone knows what is covered.

4. The functions of the trademark (CJEU)

According to the CJEU, the use of a sign identical or similar to a trademark is forbidden when it harms one of the trademark's functions:

  1. Origin: identify the origin of the product (essential function).
  2. Quality: guarantee a certain standard or level of quality.
  3. Communication / advertising: promote the company's image and identity.
  4. Investment: represent the company's financial and commercial investment in its development and reputation.

Origin function: Hoffmann-La Roche

CJEU, 23 May 1978, Hoffmann-La Roche, C-102/77, §7: "The essential function of the trademark is to guarantee the identity of the origin of the trade-marked product to the consumer or ultimate user, by enabling him without any possibility of confusion to distinguish that product from products which have another origin." Any sign confusing the consumer on origin infringes.

Beyond origin: Arsenal

CJEU, 12 Nov 2002, Arsenal Football Club, C-206/01: a retailer sold scarves bearing "Arsenal" while stating they were not official merchandise. The slides present it as follows: consumers are not misled about origin, so the club cannot automatically prohibit the sale. The slides mark this approach as "Not applicable anymore": treating origin as the only function would let third parties use others' marks whenever there is no confusion on origin.

In the actual judgment, the CJEU held that the retailer's use was liable to jeopardise the guarantee of origin, so Arsenal could prohibit it; the "disclaimer" did not help. The lasting principle of Arsenal is that the owner can only act when the use affects (or is liable to affect) the functions of the mark. For the exam, use the slides' teaching point (the functions test, origin is not the only function) and avoid stating the outcome as a certainty.

Reputation: Bellure

CJEU, 18 June 2009, Bellure, C-487/07, §58: selling perfumes with names very close to famous perfumes (slide example: "Shalimar" vs. "Shalimar Lux") to take advantage of the original brand's reputation. Taking advantage of the reputation of a famous mark for free may be prohibited. This is extended protection: beyond origin, the mark protects the company's reputation and investment.

The case is usually cited as L'Oréal v Bellure; the claimant was L'Oréal. The "Shalimar" example comes from the slides; check it against your notes before quoting it as the facts of the case.

Advertising: Google France

CJEU, 23 March 2010, Google, C-236/08 to C-238/08, §91–92: Google let advertisers buy competitors' brand names as keywords (AdWords). Use of a trademark is prohibited if it harms the mark as a promotional tool or commercial strategy (advertising function).

  • Saying the origin function is the only function. The CJEU recognises four.
  • Mixing up certification (standards set by the owner) and collective (membership of an association) marks.
  • Citing the definition without its source: always write Art. 3 Directive 2015/2436.

CHAPTERS.title: Types of trademarks
CHAPTERS.summary: The eight types of marks in the slides, plus store layouts and the special case of smell and taste marks.
CHAPTERS.html:
A sign can be registered as a trademark when it is capable of being represented and distinctive. The slides list eight types:

#Type (FR)Definition (slides)
1Word mark (marque verbale)Exclusively words, letters, numerals, other standard typographic characters, or a combination that can be typed.
2Figurative mark (marque figurative)Uses pictures, logos, special designs, colours or stylised text instead of plain words; any graphic element representing the brand.
3Shape mark (marque de forme)Consists of or extends to a three-dimensional shape; may contain word elements. Containers, packaging, the product itself or its appearance.
4Position mark (marque de position)The specific way the mark is placed or affixed on the product.
5Pattern mark (marque de motif)Exclusively a set of elements repeated regularly.
6Colour mark (marque de couleur)A single colour without contours, or a combination of colours without contours.
7Motion mark (marque de mouvement)Consists of or extends to a movement or change in position of the elements (a sequence of stills can qualify).
8Multimedia mark (marque multimédia)Combination of image and sound (example: McDonald's audiovisual ad).

The slides' "reminder" also lists the sound mark (marque sonore) among registrable signs (see chapter 5, Shield Mark).

Layout of a retail store

Can be protected as a trademark if it has acquired distinctiveness and identifies the commercial origin of the goods/services (see Apple, C-421/13, chapter 6).

Smell (olfactory) and taste marks

Extremely rare and usually not accepted, because they hardly meet the essential criteria (representation). Example given: in the United States, the smell of Play-Doh modelling clay was registered as an olfactory mark. That is US law, not EU law.

  • Confusing a position mark (where the sign is placed) with a shape mark (the 3D form itself).
  • Confusing a motion mark (movement only) with a multimedia mark (image + sound).
  • Using the Play-Doh example to say smells are registrable in the EU. They are not, in practice (see Sieckmann).

CHAPTERS.title: Validity (1): capacity of representation
CHAPTERS.summary: The two validity requirements, the Sieckmann criteria, how each type of sign must be represented, and the leading cases (Dyson, Sieckmann, Libertel, Shield Mark, strawberries).
CHAPTERS.html:
1. The two requirements (absolute grounds)

From Art. 3 Directive 2015/2436, any sign can be a trademark provided that:

  1. Distinctiveness: the sign lets its owner distinguish himself from competitors. A concept that is too vague, too generic or purely descriptive cannot be a trademark.
  2. Representation: the sign can be represented clearly and precisely, so the subject of protection is identifiable.

Failing either is an absolute ground for refusal (motif absolu de refus): the problem lies in the sign itself, whatever the rights of third parties.

2. A sign must be a precise sign, not a concept: Dyson

CJEU, 25 Jan 2007, Dyson, C-321/03: Dyson applied for a transparent dust collection bin, claiming consumers would recognise any transparent container as a Dyson. Refused: a trademark must be a precise and specific sign; Dyson was claiming a vague concept (any transparent container, whatever its shape).

3. The Sieckmann criteria

CJEU, 12 Dec 2002, Sieckmann, C-273/00: Mr Sieckmann tried to register a smell at the German Patent Office, using:

  1. a chemical formula: shows the substance, not the smell as perceived by humans;
  2. a verbal description ("balsamically fruity…"): subjective, open to interpretation;
  3. a sample of the smell: not durable, it fades or changes.

None satisfied the representation requirement. The representation must be:

CriterionMeaning (slides)
ClearPeople can easily see the trademark
PreciseNo confusion about what it covers
Self-containedShows everything needed on its own
Easily accessibleAnyone can view or find it
IntelligibleIt makes sense and is understandable
DurableIt lasts over time and still represents the brand
ObjectiveNot subjective; straightforward and neutral
Mnemonic for the 7 Sieckmann criteria: C-P-S-E-I-D-O ("Clear Precise Signs Easily Identify Durable Origins").
Sieckmann was decided when EU law required graphic representation. Directive 2015/2436 replaced this with representation "on the register" in a clear and precise manner, which allows audio and video files. The Sieckmann criteria are still used to judge whether the representation is clear and precise.

4. How to represent each type of sign

TypeWhat to file
PatternA reproduction showing the pattern of repetition; a description of how the elements repeat is allowed.
ShapeA graphic reproduction (computer-generated images allowed) or a photographic reproduction; may contain different views.
MotionA video file showing the movement, or a series of still sequential images.
Colour (single)A sample on paper is not enough: a universal colour code (Pantone, RAL…) must identify it accurately (Libertel).
Colour combinationReproduction showing the systematic arrangement (mandatory) + generally recognised colour code (mandatory) + description of the arrangement (optional).
PositionIdentification of the position and size/proportion (mandatory) + visual disclaimer of elements not claimed (mandatory) + description of how it is affixed (optional).
SoundAn audio file (MP3, max 5 MB) or an accurate musical notation. Not accepted alone: onomatopoeia, musical notes alone (e.g. E, D#, E…), a sonogram.

5. Colour marks: Libertel

Rule: a colour on its own, without shape, cannot normally be recognised as a trademark. However, for certain goods/services, when the colour is distinctive and capable of representation, it can be protected (Milka purple, Tiffany blue).

CJEU, 6 May 2003, Libertel, C-104/01: a colour sample on paper is not enough (it fades); the applicant must give an internationally recognised colour code.

6. Sound marks: Shield Mark

CJEU, 27 Nov 2003, Shield Mark BV, C-283/01: Shield Mark wanted to register sounds. Question: can a sound be a trademark and how should it be represented? Yes, if (1) the sound can distinguish the goods/services of one undertaking and (2) it is represented in a clear, precise, durable… way (e.g. a stave divided into bars with clef and notes). Onomatopoeia or a list of notes alone are not enough.

Steps to register a sound (slides): identify the sound clearly; submit an audio file (MP3, max 5 MB) or musical notation; show it is distinctive (not a generic sound).

7. Smell marks: the ripe strawberry

General Court (TUE), 27 Oct 2005, Smell of ripe strawberries, T-305/04: Eden SARL applied for the "smell of ripe strawberries" using a verbal description and a colour image of a strawberry. Refused: the subject of protection cannot be determined with clarity and precision with generally available technology, so the sign is not capable of representation.

To sum up: as long as it is capable of representation, a trademark can be a sound, a movement, a video, a colour, etc. A taste or smell cannot, because it cannot be represented clearly and precisely.

8. Slide exercises (what do you think?)

  • Linda wants to register the colour pink.
  • Georges wants to register the mooing of a cow, represented by a sonogram.
  • Linda wants to register an orange strip covering the toe area of a sock.
  • Bill wants to register the shape of an egg for cosmetics.

Worked answers are in Practical cases → "Can they register it?".

  • Saying a colour sample is enough. It is not: you need a colour code (Libertel).
  • Filing a sound as a sonogram or onomatopoeia alone. Use an audio file or musical notation.
  • Mixing up the two requirements: Dyson is about a concept that is not a sign; Sieckmann is about representation.

CHAPTERS.title: Validity (2): distinctiveness
CHAPTERS.summary: Definition (Art. 7(1)(b) EU Regulation), the four non-distinctive categories (Art. 4 Directive), how it is assessed, acquired distinctiveness, slogans, store layouts, shapes and the three shape exclusions, Louboutin.
CHAPTERS.html:
1. Definition

Distinctiveness allows (1) the trademark owner to be identified and (2) the market players to be differentiated. The sign must lead the relevant public to believe that the goods or services originate from a particular company.

Art. 7(1)(b) EU Trademark Regulation sets the definition: the sign serves to identify the goods/services for which registration is applied for, so it determines their origin and distinguishes them from others.

The slides say "EU regulation on trademark". Its full name is Regulation (EU) 2017/1001 on the European Union trade mark (EUTMR). Article 7(1)(b) is literally the refusal of marks "devoid of any distinctive character".

Principle of specialty: a trademark is protected only for the goods/services for which it is registered, so the sign must be distinctive towards those goods/services.

2. Signs that are not distinctive (Art. 4 Directive 2015/2436)

Article 4 lists the grounds for refusal or invalidity. A sign is not distinctive if it is:

CategoryMeaningExamples (slides)
1. Devoid of any distinctive characterDoes not allow the product to be recognised as coming from a particular company: too generic or common"Shoes" for shoes, "Food" for a restaurant, "the coffee" to sell coffee
2. DescriptiveConsists exclusively of signs which may serve in trade to designate a characteristic: kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin, date of production"Red Wine from Bordeaux" for wine, "Soft Soap" for soap
3. Customary (too common)Consists exclusively of signs that have become customary in current language or established trade practices"Cola" for a soft drink, "pack" to sell bags
4. Bad faithA mark filed in bad faith may also be declared invalid(no example in the slides)

Slide summary: not distinctive if the sign (1) designates the goods (generic: "bags" for bags), (2) refers to a characteristic (descriptive: "leather" for leather bags, "cola" for a cola drink), (3) is commonly used to designate them ("pack" for bags).

3. How distinctiveness is assessed (French law, slides)

  1. In relation to the goods and services for which registration is sought;
  2. according to the presumed perception of the average consumer of those goods/services.

Examples: Apple is distinctive for computers and phones but not for fruit. "Eco-Net" for eco-friendly cleaning products was refused: the average consumer immediately understands "environmentally friendly cleaning".

4. Baby-Dry

CJCE, 20 Sept 2001, Baby-Dry, C-383/99 P: the slides say the CJEU refused "BABY-DRY" for nappies as too descriptive.

In the actual judgment (Procter & Gamble v OHIM), the Court of Justice set aside the refusal: it found "Baby-dry" was an unusual juxtaposition of words, not exclusively descriptive, so it could be registered. Later case law became stricter on descriptive marks. Ask your professor which version is expected; in the exam you can write "the slides present Baby-Dry as…" and show you know the real outcome.

5. Distinctiveness acquired through use

A sign that is generic, descriptive or customary can still be registered if it "has become distinctive in relation to the goods or services for which registration is requested in consequence of the use which has been made of it". The sign is registered only if proof is provided.

  • Examples: L'Équipe (sports newspaper), Milka's purple, Nike's "Just do it".
  • Usually shown by: strong brand awareness, exclusive use over a long period, tangible evidence (surveys/polls, market share, advertising, turnover).
  • Assessed in relation to the perception of the average consumer for the category of goods/services concerned.
Acquired distinctiveness can cure the three categories listed on the slide (generic/devoid, descriptive, customary). Under EU law it cannot cure the shape exclusions below, public policy or deceptiveness.

6. Special signs

Store layout: Apple

CJEU, 10 July 2014, Apple, C-421/13: can the layout of a retail store be registered? Yes, if distinctive: it must help consumers recognise the origin of the goods/services and be more than a simple store design. Apple's minimalist layout (big tables, lots of space, identical worldwide) says "You are in an Apple store". Not protectable: a merely functional or generic layout.

Slogan: Vorsprung durch Technik

CJEU, 21 Jan 2010, Vorsprung durch Technik (Audi): can an advertising slogan be registered even if it has a promotional meaning? Yes, if distinctive: consumers must see it as indicating origin. Memorable, creative slogans that identify the company ("Just do it" for Nike, "Das Auto" for Volkswagen in the slides).

The case number (C-398/08 P) is not on the slides.

Shape: Lindt

CJEU, 24 May 2012, Lindt, C-98/11 P: can the shape of a product (the gold-wrapped chocolate bunny) be a trademark? In principle yes, if it is distinctive, not just functional, helps consumers recognise the origin and is not the normal or necessary shape. Applied to Lindt: refused. The bunny lacked inherent distinctiveness; its elements are too common on the market to identify Lindt across the whole EU.

7. The three shape exclusions

A shape (or another characteristic) cannot be a valid trademark when it:

ExclusionPurposeExample (slides)
1. Results from the nature of the goodsPrevent appropriation of what is natural or inherent to the productShape of a chocolate bar
2. Is necessary to obtain a technical resultNo monopoly on functional solutions (that is the role of patents, limited in time)Lego bricks (interlocking)
3. Gives substantial value to the goodsNo monopoly on aesthetic features that make the product attractive (role of designs, limited in time)Panton chair (written "pantone chair" on the slide)
Rationale: trademarks last indefinitely. The Directive prevents trademark law from granting a perpetual monopoly on technical solutions (patent territory) or aesthetic characteristics (design territory).
The Lego case is CJEU, 14 Sept 2010, Lego Juris, C-48/09 P (not on the slides).

8. Position: Louboutin

CJEU, 12 June 2018, Louboutin, C-163/16: Louboutin registered the red colour applied to the sole of high heels. A Dutch company, Van Haren, sold heels with red soles; Louboutin sued for infringement. Van Haren challenged validity, arguing the mark was a shape giving substantial value to the product. Louboutin won: the mark protects a colour in a specific position, not a shape, so the shape exclusion does not apply.

9. Slide exercise: Pierre's drop-shipping

Pierre wants to sell phone and AirPods cases bearing Coca-Cola, Starbucks and Disney characters. Can he? How can he do it legally? Worked answer in Practical cases.

  • Assessing distinctiveness in the abstract. Always assess it for the goods/services claimed and through the average consumer.
  • Saying Lindt won. The principle was accepted but the bunny was refused.
  • Calling Louboutin a shape mark. It is a colour applied to a position.
  • Forgetting to mention acquired distinctiveness as the way to save a weak sign.

CHAPTERS.title: Other absolute grounds: public policy, flags, deceptive signs
CHAPTERS.summary: Signs contrary to public policy or morality, flags and state emblems, deceptive signs, and the wrap-up exercises (Exercise 2, Sarah's cosmetics, group project).
CHAPTERS.html:
1. Public policy and morality

Trademarks contrary to public policy or to accepted principles of morality (ordre public, bonnes mœurs) cannot be registered.

SignPublicOutcomeRef.
BIN LADINGeneral consumerRejected: understood as the name of the leader of a terrorist organisation; terrorist crimes breach public order and moral principlesR 176/2004-2
SCREW YOU (goods other than sex products)General consumerRejected: a substantial proportion of ordinary citizens would find it offensiveR 495/2005-G
SCREW YOU (sex products)Sex-shop customersAccepted: a person entering a sex shop is unlikely to be offendedR 495/2005-G
The assessment depends on the goods and services concerned, which determine the public targeted and its perception.
The "R …" numbers are EUIPO Board of Appeal decisions (as shown on the slides).

2. Flags, state emblems and similar signs

Trademarks including flags, (state) emblems, badges, armorial bearings or escutcheons of particular public interest cannot be registered, unless the competent authority has consented.

3. Deceptive signs

A deceptive sign (signe déceptif) cannot be registered: it aims to or could deceive the public on the nature, quality or geographical origin of the goods or services.

Example: "OrganicFresh" on apples that are not organic: misleads consumers into thinking they are organic.

Descriptive vs. deceptive: "Organic" for organic apples is descriptive (true but not distinctive); "Organic" for non-organic apples is deceptive (false). The same word can fall on either side depending on the goods.

4. Wrap-up exercises from the slides

  • Exercise 2: FreshMilk for pasteurised milk; a blue sole for trainers; SugarFree for sweets containing sugar; LuxuryBag for handbags.
  • Case study: Sarah's cosmetics (7 signs: "Beauty Cares", "Beautiful", the colour white, bubbles in motion, a cat's meow, "Cannabis", "Milky care"). Advise on absolute grounds, representation, and the strongest mark.
  • Group project (slide 200): create your own trademark in 4/5 Canva slides: justify validity, what you protected, what you could not protect.

All are worked in Practical cases.

  • Treating public policy as absolute in the abstract. It depends on the goods and the relevant public (SCREW YOU).
  • Forgetting the consent exception for flags and emblems.
  • Confusing descriptive and deceptive.

CASES.name: Hoffmann-La Roche
CASES.facts: Dispute over the use of a trademark on (re)packaged pharmaceutical products.
CASES.question: What is the essential function of a trademark?
CASES.holding: The essential function is to guarantee the identity of the origin of the trade-marked product to the consumer, enabling him without any possibility of confusion to distinguish it from products of another origin.
CASES.why: Founding definition of the origin function. Quote it whenever you discuss what a trademark is for.
CASES.flag: The facts line is a general description; the slides only quote §7.

CASES.name: Arsenal Football Club
CASES.facts: A retailer (Mr Reed) sold scarves bearing "Arsenal" with a notice that they were not official club products.
CASES.question: Can the trademark owner prohibit use of an identical sign when consumers are not misled about origin?
CASES.holding: Slides: the club cannot automatically prohibit the sale if consumers are not misled; this origin-only approach is "not applicable anymore". The owner can act when the use affects the functions of the mark.
CASES.why: Shows the move from origin as the only function to a functions test. Also cited for double identity (identical sign, identical goods).
CASES.flag: In the actual judgment the CJEU found the use was liable to affect the guarantee of origin, so Arsenal could prohibit it. Check which reading your professor expects.

CASES.name: Bellure (L'Oréal v Bellure)
CASES.facts: Perfumes sold under names and presentations close to famous perfumes (slide example: "Shalimar" vs. "Shalimar Lux") to ride on their reputation.
CASES.question: Is taking advantage of a famous mark's reputation, without confusion, prohibited?
CASES.holding: Yes. Taking unfair advantage (a free ride) of the reputation of a famous mark may be prohibited, even without confusion on origin.
CASES.why: Extended protection: trademarks also protect reputation and investment, not only origin.
CASES.flag: The claimant was L'Oréal; the Shalimar example comes from the slides.

CASES.name: Google France
CASES.facts: Google's AdWords let advertisers buy competitors' brand names as keywords.
CASES.question: Can keyword use of a trademark harm the mark?
CASES.holding: Use of a trademark is prohibited if it harms the mark as a promotional tool or commercial strategy (advertising function).

CASES.name: Dyson
CASES.facts: Dyson applied to register a transparent dust-collection bin, claiming any transparent container would be recognised as Dyson.
CASES.question: Can a non-specific characteristic (transparency) of a product be a trademark?
CASES.holding: No. A trademark must be a precise and specific sign; Dyson claimed a vague concept covering all shapes of transparent bins.
CASES.why: A concept or idea is not a sign. Use it when an applicant claims something abstract.

CASES.name: Sieckmann
CASES.facts: Mr Sieckmann tried to register a smell at the German Patent Office using a chemical formula, a verbal description ("balsamically fruity") and a sample.
CASES.question: Can a smell be represented in a way that satisfies trademark law?
CASES.holding: No. The formula shows the substance, not the smell; the description is subjective; the sample is not durable. The representation must be clear, precise, self-contained, easily accessible, intelligible, durable and objective.
CASES.why: The 7 Sieckmann criteria: the test for every representation question.

CASES.name: Libertel
CASES.facts: Application to register a colour (orange) per se, filed with a sample on paper.
CASES.question: Can a colour per se be a trademark, and how must it be represented?
CASES.holding: A colour can be a trademark if distinctive, but a paper sample is not enough (not durable): an internationally recognised colour code must be given.
CASES.why: Colour marks: sample + colour code (Pantone, RAL…). Distinctiveness of a single colour is rare without use.
CASES.flag: The colour (orange) and the facts are not on the slides.

CASES.name: Shield Mark BV
CASES.facts: Shield Mark wanted to register sounds to stand out from competitors.
CASES.question: Can a sound be a trademark, and how should it be represented?
CASES.holding: Yes, if it can distinguish goods/services and is represented clearly, precisely, durably (e.g. musical notation). Onomatopoeia or a list of notes alone are not enough.
CASES.why: Sound marks. Today: audio file (MP3, max 5 MB) or musical notation; not a sonogram or onomatopoeia alone.

CASES.name: Smell of ripe strawberries
CASES.facts: Eden SARL applied for the "smell of ripe strawberries" with a verbal description and a colour picture of a strawberry.
CASES.question: Is this a sufficient representation of an olfactory sign?
CASES.holding: No. The subject of protection cannot be determined clearly and precisely with generally available technology, so the sign is not capable of representation.
CASES.why: Confirms Sieckmann: smell marks are not registrable in practice in the EU.

CASES.name: Baby-Dry
CASES.facts: Procter & Gamble applied for "BABY-DRY" for baby nappies.
CASES.question: Is a combination of descriptive words registrable?
CASES.holding: Slides: refused as too descriptive of the product.
CASES.why: Illustrates descriptive signs in the slides.
CASES.flag: In the actual judgment, the Court set aside the refusal: the unusual juxtaposition was not exclusively descriptive, so the mark was registrable. Check with your professor.

CASES.name: Apple (store layout)
CASES.facts: Apple sought to register the layout of its flagship stores (minimalist design, big tables, identical worldwide).
CASES.question: Can the layout of a retail store be registered as a trademark?
CASES.holding: Yes, if it is distinctive: it must help consumers recognise the origin and be more than a simple functional or generic store design.
CASES.why: Store layouts are registrable signs, subject to distinctiveness.

CASES.name: Vorsprung durch Technik (Audi)
CASES.facts: Audi applied for its slogan "Vorsprung durch Technik" (advancement through technology).
CASES.question: Can an advertising slogan be registered even if it has a promotional meaning?
CASES.holding: Yes, if consumers can perceive it as indicating the origin of the goods/services. Promotional character alone does not exclude registration.
CASES.why: Slogans: memorable, creative, identify the company (Just do it).
CASES.flag: Case number not on the slides.

CASES.name: Lindt (gold bunny)
CASES.facts: Lindt tried to register the 3D shape of its gold-wrapped chocolate bunny with a red ribbon as an EU trademark.
CASES.question: Can the shape of a product be a trademark?
CASES.holding: In principle yes, if distinctive and not just functional or the usual shape. Here: refused, the shape lacked inherent distinctiveness; its elements are too common to identify Lindt across the EU.
CASES.why: Shape marks: must depart from what is common in the sector; distinctiveness must exist across the whole EU for an EU mark.

CASES.name: Lego (brick)
CASES.facts: Registration of the shape of the Lego brick.
CASES.question: Can a shape necessary to obtain a technical result be a trademark?
CASES.holding: No. The brick's shape is necessary to achieve the technical result (interlocking).
CASES.why: Second shape exclusion: functional shapes belong to patent law, limited in time.
CASES.flag: The slides only say "Lego bricks were refused"; date and number are not on the slides.

CASES.name: Louboutin
CASES.facts: Louboutin registered the red colour applied to the sole of high heels. Van Haren sold red-soled heels; Louboutin sued; Van Haren argued the mark was a shape giving substantial value.
CASES.question: Is a colour applied to the sole of a shoe a "shape" caught by the shape exclusions?
CASES.holding: No. The mark protects a colour in a specific position, not a shape; the shape exclusion does not apply. Louboutin won.
CASES.why: Position/colour marks escape the shape exclusions.

CASES.name: BIN LADIN
CASES.facts: Application for "BIN LADIN" for general consumer goods.
CASES.question: Is the sign contrary to public policy or morality?
CASES.holding: Rejected: understood as the name of the leader of a terrorist organisation; contrary to public order and moral principles.

CASES.name: SCREW YOU
CASES.facts: Application for "SCREW YOU" for various goods, including sex products.
CASES.question: Does the morality assessment depend on the goods?
CASES.holding: Rejected for general goods (offensive to ordinary citizens) but accepted for sex products (sex-shop customers unlikely to be offended).
CASES.why: Public policy/morality is assessed according to the goods and the relevant public.

CARDS: Ownership of a creation that has no physical form (e.g. a trademark) or is a product of the human mind (software, book, poem). Opposed to ownership of tangible goods.
What does an IP right give its holder?
An exclusive right to exploit the creation (use, reproduce, distribute, commercially exploit) and to prohibit others from doing so, for a limited time and within a defined territory.
The four aims of IP law?
1. Protect creators (exclusive right). 2. Promote innovation, creativity, investment. 3. Financial incentives + prevent copying. 4. Guarantee the quality of products for consumers.
The two branches of IP in French law?
Literary and artistic property (copyright, software, databases) and industrial property (patents, trademarks, designs). Rules in the Intellectual Property Code (CPI).
Novelty, inventive step, industrial application (slides also: technological field). 20 years from filing, annual fees.
Novelty + individual character. 5 years, renewable up to 25 years.
Original work (author's personal touch), expressed (not just an idea). Author's life + 70 years.
PDO (AOP): principal production steps in the same area (Champagne). PGI (IGP): quality/reputation/characteristics linked to origin (Bayonne ham).
IG for industrial and hand-crafted products: example?
Registered company name, commercial name, domain name.
How are company names, commercial names and domain names protected?
No common legislation; only through a tort action (responsabilité délictuelle) for unfair competition (concurrence déloyale), not infringement (contrefaçon).
Conditions to protect a commercial name?
Use where the name is registered, of an identical/similar sign, for an identical/similar activity, in the same geographical area, likely to create confusion.
A distinctive sign is only protected for the goods and services for which it is used/registered (e.g. Sandro for fashion).
Inditex, Zara, zara.fr: which sign is which?
Inditex = registered company name; Zara = trademark/commercial name; zara.fr = domain name.
Art. 3 Directive 2015/2436: any sign capable of (a) distinguishing goods/services of one undertaking from others and (b) being represented on the register clearly and precisely.
Sign showing goods/services comply with standards set by the owner (quality, materials, manufacture…). E.g. Fairtrade.
Sign distinguishing goods/services of members of an association that owns it; shows membership. E.g. Vignerons indépendants.
The four functions of a trademark (CJEU)?
Essential function = guarantee the identity of origin of the product to the consumer.
Taking unfair advantage of the reputation of a famous mark may be prohibited, even without confusion. Extended protection.
Keyword use of a mark is prohibited if it harms the mark as a promotional/advertising tool.
The eight types of marks in the slides?
Word, figurative, shape, position, pattern, colour, motion, multimedia (+ sound in the reminder; store layout).
The specific way the mark is placed or affixed on the product (e.g. Louboutin red sole).
Smell and taste marks in the EU?
Extremely rare, usually refused: cannot be represented clearly and precisely. (Play-Doh smell was registered in the US.)
Clear, precise, self-contained, easily accessible, intelligible, durable, objective.
Chemical formula = substance not smell; verbal description = subjective; sample = not durable.
Transparent bin refused: a vague concept, not a precise and specific sign.
Colour mark: a sample on paper is not enough; give an internationally recognised colour code.
A sound can be a mark if distinctive and represented clearly (musical notation/audio). Not onomatopoeia or notes alone.
Smell of ripe strawberries refused: cannot be represented clearly and precisely with generally available technology.
How to file a position mark?
Mandatory: position and size + visual disclaimer of unclaimed elements. Optional: description.
How to file a colour combination?
Mandatory: reproduction of the systematic arrangement + recognised colour code. Optional: description.
How to file a motion mark?
Video file or series of still sequential images.
How to file a sound mark?
Audio file (MP3, max 5 MB) or accurate musical notation. Not alone: onomatopoeia, notes alone, sonogram.
Art. 7(1)(b) EU Trademark Regulation: the sign identifies the goods/services and their origin.
Four categories of non-distinctive signs (Art. 4 Directive)?
Devoid of distinctive character; descriptive; customary; (and bad-faith marks may be invalidated).
Consists exclusively of indications of kind, quality, quantity, purpose, value, origin… e.g. "Soft Soap" for soap.
"Cola" for a soft drink; "pack" for bags.
1. The goods/services claimed. 2. The presumed perception of the average consumer.
Long, exclusive use; brand awareness; surveys/polls, market share, advertising, turnover.
A store layout can be a mark if distinctive (identifies origin), not a merely functional/generic layout.
A slogan can be registered if consumers see it as an indication of origin, despite its promotional meaning.
Refused: the gold bunny lacked inherent distinctiveness (too common across the EU).
Shape resulting from the nature of the goods; necessary for a technical result; giving substantial value to the goods.
Avoid a perpetual trademark monopoly on technical (patent) or aesthetic (design) features.
Red sole valid: a colour in a position, not a shape giving substantial value. Louboutin beat Van Haren.
Baby-Dry: what do the slides say?
Refused as too descriptive for nappies. (Actual judgment: the CJEU allowed it. Check with your professor.)
BIN LADIN (rejected). SCREW YOU: rejected for general goods, accepted for sex products.
Cannot be registered unless the competent authority consents.
Deceives the public on the nature, quality or geographical origin. E.g. OrganicFresh for non-organic apples.
Descriptive = true characteristic (not distinctive). Deceptive = false characteristic (misleads).
QUIZ: Intellectual property is best defined as the ownership of…
Tangible goods such as a car or a house
Creations without physical form or products of the human mind
Any good registered with a public authority
Only inventions protected by a patent
IP is defined by opposition to the ownership of physical goods: it covers intangible creations (a trademark) and products of the mind (software, a book).
Under French law, trademarks belong to…
French law splits IP into literary and artistic property (copyright, software, databases) and industrial property (patents, trademarks, designs).
Which is NOT one of the aims of IP law listed in the course?
Protecting creators with an exclusive right
Guaranteeing the quality of products for consumers
The four aims: protect creators, promote innovation/investment, financial incentives and preventing copying, guarantee quality. Low prices is not one.
How long does a trademark registration last?
Trademark: 10 years, renewable indefinitely. 5→25 years is design, 20 years is patent, life+70 is copyright.
The conditions for a design are…
Design = novelty + individual character. Originality is copyright; inventive step is patent; distinctiveness is trademark.
Slide 46: Bayonne ham = PGI (quality/reputation linked to origin). Champagne = PDO; Limoges porcelain = IG for industrial and hand-crafted products.
Only the holder may exploit it for a certain period of time and within a defined territory.
Launching the clothing brand YBX and registering it protects…
The brand and all the clothing designs
The brand itself, not the common designs
Slide example: the registration protects the brand; the common designs of the clothes are not protected by the trademark.
Inditex is the legal name of the company registered with the authorities.
A merchant whose commercial name is copied by a neighbour sues on the ground of…
Other distinctive signs have no common legislation: protection only via tort, for unfair competition, not IP infringement.
Which condition is specific to commercial names and domain names, compared to company names?
Company names are protected against use in France; commercial and domain names add the condition of the same geographical area of activity.
A sign is protected for all goods once registered
A sign is protected only for the goods/services for which it is used or registered
Only special signs can be protected
Only specialised offices can register marks
E.g. Sandro is only protected for fashion items.
True or false: the owner of a domain name can sue a copier for trademark infringement on the basis of the domain name alone.
False: a domain name is not an IP right; the action is in tort (unfair competition).
Alphabet Inc. is the registered name; Google is the brand/commercial name; google.com the domain.
Under Art. 3 Directive 2015/2436, a sign must be capable of…
Distinguishing goods/services and being represented on the register
Being registered in at least two countries
Two criteria: distinctiveness + capacity of representation.
Certification mark: goods comply with standards set by the owner.
A mark owned by an association and used by its members to show membership is…
According to Hoffmann-La Roche, the essential function of a trademark is to…
C-102/77: guarantee the identity of origin of the product to the consumer.
Which case recognises protection against taking unfair advantage of a famous mark's reputation?
Bellure, C-487/07 (2009): free-riding on reputation may be prohibited.
Google France (C-236/08) is mainly about which function?
Use of brand names as keywords harming the mark as a promotional tool.
Which is NOT a trademark function recognised by the CJEU in the course?
The four: origin, quality, communication/advertising, investment.
What lesson do the slides draw from Arsenal?
Origin is the only function of a mark
Treating origin as the only function is no longer the approach
A trademark can never be used by retailers
The slides mark the origin-only approach as "not applicable anymore": the mark protects several functions.
A mark consisting of the specific way a sign is affixed on the product is a…
A combination of image and sound is a…
A set of elements repeated regularly is a…
Words, letters, numerals or characters that can be typed
Standard typographic characters that can be typed. Stylised text is figurative.
Smell marks in the EU are…
Registrable if a sample is filed
Practically not registrable for lack of clear representation
Sieckmann and the strawberry case. The Play-Doh example is US law.
A retail store layout can be a trademark…
If it is distinctive and identifies commercial origin
Which is NOT a Sieckmann criterion?
Clear, precise, self-contained, easily accessible, intelligible, durable, objective.
In Sieckmann, why did the chemical formula fail?
It shows the substance, not the smell
The formula represents the substance, not the odour perceived by humans.
Dyson's transparent bin was refused because…
It claimed a concept, not a precise sign
C-321/03: any transparent container whatever its shape = a concept.
To register a single colour (Libertel), you must file…
Paper sample alone is not enough; give a code (Pantone, RAL).
Which is accepted alone to represent a sound mark?
Notes listed as letters (E, D#, E…)
Audio file (max 5 MB) or accurate musical notation.
The ripe strawberry smell (T-305/04) was refused because…
It could not be represented clearly and precisely
Not capable of representation with generally available technology.
For a position mark, which element is optional?
Description of how the sign is affixed
Position + size and the visual disclaimer are mandatory; the description is optional.
A motion mark is represented by…
A video file or a series of still images
Refusal for lack of representation is…
Representation and distinctiveness are intrinsic conditions: absolute grounds.
Distinctiveness is assessed in relation to…
The goods/services claimed and the average consumer's perception
Two parameters: the goods/services and the presumed perception of the average consumer.
Apple is distinctive for computers, not for apples.
Describes a characteristic (quality) of the product.
Slides: a word that has become common for this type of drink.
The age of the company only
Tangible evidence of public recognition after long, exclusive use.
In Vorsprung durch Technik, the CJEU held that a slogan…
Can be registered if perceived as indicating origin
Promotional meaning does not exclude registration if the slogan indicates origin.
Refused for lack of inherent distinctiveness
Refused as contrary to public policy
C-98/11 P: too common on the market to identify Lindt across the EU.
The Lego brick shape was refused because it…
Results from the nature of the goods
Is necessary to obtain a technical result
A designer chair whose shape is the main reason people buy it falls under…
Shape giving substantial value (Panton chair example).
Why does EU law exclude certain shapes from trademark protection?
To avoid perpetual monopolies on technical or aesthetic features
Those features belong to patents/designs, which are limited in time.
In Louboutin (C-163/16), the red sole was upheld because…
It is a colour in a specific position, not a shape
Van Haren acted in bad faith
Not a shape giving substantial value: a colour applied to a position.
According to the slides, which of these is listed in Art. 4 Directive as making a mark liable to be declared invalid?
Devoid, descriptive, customary, and bad faith.
"Eco-Net" for eco-friendly cleaning products was refused because…
The average consumer immediately understands it as eco-friendly cleaning
Perception of the average consumer: descriptive.
True or false: a descriptive sign can never become a trademark.
False: it can be registered if it has acquired distinctiveness through use (with proof).
Which one CANNOT be cured by acquired distinctiveness?
A shape necessary to obtain a technical result
A sign devoid of distinctive character
The slides list only generic/descriptive/customary signs as curable by use. Shape exclusions are not (beyond-slides confirmation: EU law).
Contrary to public policy and morality
What does the SCREW YOU decision show?
Offensive words can never be registered
Morality is assessed according to the goods and the relevant public
Only the EUIPO can refuse marks
Refused for general goods, accepted for sex products.
A national flag in a trademark can be registered…
With the consent of the competent authority
Flags, state emblems, badges, armorial bearings: refused unless the authority consents.
Misleads on the nature/quality of the goods.
"OrganicFresh" for organic apples would most likely be refused as…
If the apples are organic, the sign is true: descriptive (not distinctive). For non-organic apples it would be deceptive.
Describes the goods and their quality.
Deceptive signs mislead the public on…
The identity of the applicant's lawyer
Nature, quality or geographical origin of the goods/services.

PRACTICE.title: Can they register it?
PRACTICE.facts:
Four clients come to you for advice:
  1. Linda wants to register the colour pink (a pink square, no contour).
  2. Georges wants to register the mooing of a cow and files a sonogram.
  3. Linda wants to register an orange strip covering the toe area of a sock.
  4. Bill wants to register the shape of an egg for cosmetics (e.g. a lip balm).
tasks: For each sign: which type of mark is it?
Is it capable of representation, and what exactly must be filed?
Is it distinctive for the goods? What risk remains?
hints: Start with the type of mark, then apply the representation rules for that type (chapter 5 table), then distinctiveness.
Libertel for colours, Shield Mark for sounds, the position-mark filing rules, and the shape rules + Lindt for the egg.
PRACTICE.model:
Issue
Can each sign meet the two absolute requirements of Art. 3 Directive 2015/2436: capacity of representation and distinctiveness?
Rule
Representation must be clear, precise, self-contained, easily accessible, intelligible, durable and objective (Sieckmann, C-273/00). Distinctiveness is assessed for the goods claimed and through the average consumer (Art. 7(1)(b) EUTMR, Art. 4 Directive).
Application

1. Pink (colour mark). A paper sample is not enough; Linda must file the colour with an internationally recognised code such as Pantone or RAL (Libertel, C-104/01). Distinctiveness is the real problem: a single colour without contour is in principle not distinctive. It can be accepted only if consumers associate it with her (acquired distinctiveness, like Milka purple or Tiffany blue), proven by surveys, market share, advertising and turnover. The answer also depends on the goods: pink is very common for cosmetics or baby products.

2. Cow mooing (sound mark). A sonogram alone is not accepted. Georges must file an audio file (MP3, max 5 MB) or an accurate musical notation (Shield Mark, C-283/01). Distinctiveness depends on the goods: for dairy products a cow's moo is close to descriptive and probably refused; for unrelated goods (e.g. software) it is arbitrary and can be distinctive.

3. Orange strip on the toe (position mark). Linda must identify the position and the size/proportion of the strip, and add a visual disclaimer (for instance dotted lines for the sock itself, which is not claimed); a description is optional. Distinctiveness: a coloured toe can be decorative, so she must show consumers see it as an indication of origin, by analogy with Louboutin's red sole (C-163/16), which was upheld as a colour in a specific position.

4. Egg shape (shape mark). File a graphic or photographic reproduction, possibly with several views. Check the three exclusions: an egg shape is not imposed by the nature of a lip balm, does not seem necessary for a technical result, but if the shape is the main reason people buy it, the "substantial value" exclusion is a risk. Distinctiveness: like Lindt (C-98/11 P), the shape must depart from what is common in the sector, otherwise it is refused; acquired distinctiveness is possible for the inherent-distinctiveness problem but not for the shape exclusions.

Conclusion
All four signs can be represented if filed correctly (not the sonogram). The main risk for each is distinctiveness. Practical advice: file correctly, gather evidence of use, and combine the sign with a distinctive word mark to secure protection immediately.

PRACTICE.title: Are these trademarks valid?
PRACTICE.facts:
Do you think these trademarks are valid?
  1. FreshMilk for pasteurised milk
  2. A blue sole for trainers
  3. SugarFree for sweets containing sugar
  4. LuxuryBag for handbags
tasks: Identify the absolute ground at stake for each sign.
Conclude: valid, invalid, or valid under conditions?
hints: Two are about describing the product, one is about lying about the product, one is a position mark.
Descriptive vs deceptive; for the blue sole, think Louboutin and acquired distinctiveness.
PRACTICE.model:
Issue
Does each sign escape the absolute grounds for refusal (lack of distinctiveness, deceptiveness)?
Rule
Art. 4 Directive 2015/2436: signs devoid of distinctive character, descriptive or customary signs are refused, unless distinctiveness is acquired by use. Deceptive signs (nature, quality, geographical origin) are refused.
Application

FreshMilk: describes the kind and a quality of the product (milk, fresh). Descriptive, so not distinctive. Refused unless Fresh Milk proves acquired distinctiveness.

Blue sole for trainers: a position mark (colour in a specific place). Not a shape, so the shape exclusions do not apply (Louboutin, C-163/16). Validity depends on distinctiveness: if blue soles are common for trainers, consumers will not see an indication of origin; registration then needs acquired distinctiveness. File: position and size + visual disclaimer + colour code.

SugarFree for sweets containing sugar: deceives the public on the nature/quality of the goods. Refused as deceptive. (For sugar-free sweets, it would instead be descriptive.)

LuxuryBag for handbags: "bag" designates the goods and "luxury" is laudatory. Descriptive / devoid of distinctive character. Refused.

Conclusion
Only the blue sole can be valid, provided it is distinctive (possibly acquired by use). The three word signs are refused; advice: choose an arbitrary or invented word.

PRACTICE.title: Sarah's cosmetics brand
PRACTICE.facts:
Sarah runs a cosmetics company (perfumery, body and face care, make-up). She is considering several signs:
  1. The words "Beauty Cares"
  2. The word "Beautiful"
  3. The colour white
  4. Bubbles in motion
  5. The meowing of a cat
  6. The word "Cannabis"
  7. The words "Milky care"
tasks: Advise on the intrinsic validity of each sign for cosmetics: are there absolute grounds for refusal?
What representation must she submit for each?
Which would make the strongest trademark?
hints: For each sign: type of mark → representation → distinctiveness for cosmetics → other absolute grounds (public policy, deceptive).
"Cannabis" raises public policy and descriptive/deceptive questions; "Milky care" depends on whether the products contain milk; the strongest mark is the most arbitrary one for cosmetics.
PRACTICE.model:
Issue
Are these signs valid trademarks for cosmetics under the absolute grounds, and how should each be represented?
Rule
Sign capable of distinguishing and of being represented (Art. 3 Directive 2015/2436); Sieckmann criteria; refusal of signs devoid of distinctive character, descriptive or customary (Art. 4 Directive, Art. 7(1)(b) EUTMR), unless acquired distinctiveness; refusal of signs contrary to public policy/morality and deceptive signs. Distinctiveness is assessed for cosmetics and through the average consumer.
Application

1. "Beauty Cares" (word mark: typed text). Describes the purpose of the goods (caring for beauty). Descriptive and laudatory: likely refused, unless acquired distinctiveness.

2. "Beautiful" (word mark). A laudatory word everyone uses for cosmetics: devoid of distinctive character / customary. Refused.

3. The colour white (colour mark: sample + recognised colour code, Libertel). A single colour, very common for cosmetics packaging and creams: devoid of distinctive character. Only possible with strong proof of acquired distinctiveness (Milka-type evidence). Weak.

4. Bubbles in motion (motion mark: video file or sequence of stills). For soaps and shower gels, bubbles describe foam: weak/descriptive. For make-up or perfume, more arbitrary and potentially distinctive. Arguable: depends on the goods claimed.

5. A cat's meow (sound mark: audio file MP3 ≤ 5 MB or musical notation; not onomatopoeia like "meow", not a sonogram, per Shield Mark). Arbitrary for cosmetics, so distinctive. Strong candidate.

6. "Cannabis" (word mark). Several risks: public policy (reference to a drug, especially if the public perceives it as promoting it); if the products contain hemp, the word is descriptive; if they do not, deceptive. Strong refusal risk.

EU decisions have refused cannabis-related signs on public-policy grounds, but no such case is in the slides. Verify before citing one.

7. "Milky care" (word mark). If the products contain milk: descriptive of an ingredient and purpose. If they do not: deceptive as to the nature/composition. Weak either way.

Conclusion
The strongest mark is the cat's meow (arbitrary for cosmetics), followed by bubbles in motion for make-up/perfume only. Recommended action: register the sound mark correctly represented, and pair it with an invented word mark (the strongest kind of sign), rather than descriptive words like "Beauty Cares" or "Beautiful".

PRACTICE.title: Pierre's drop-shipping cases
PRACTICE.facts: Pierre wants to sell phone cases and AirPods cases online through drop-shipping. The products bear the trademarks Coca-Cola, Starbucks and Disney characters.
tasks: Can he do that legally speaking?
How can he do it legally?
hints: Think about what the owner's exclusive right covers and which functions of these marks are affected.
These are famous marks: Bellure and the reputation/investment functions. The legal route is the owner's authorisation.
PRACTICE.model:
Issue
Can Pierre use other companies' famous trademarks on products he sells without their authorisation?
Rule
The trademark owner has an exclusive right over the commercial exploitation of the sign and can prohibit any use without authorisation (chapter 1). Use of an identical or similar sign is prohibited when it harms one of the trademark's functions: origin, quality, advertising, investment (Hoffmann-La Roche; Arsenal). Taking unfair advantage of the reputation of a famous mark is prohibited even without confusion (Bellure, C-487/07).
Application
Coca-Cola, Starbucks and Disney are registered, famous marks. Pierre would be selling goods bearing identical signs in the course of trade, without consent. Consumers may believe the cases are official merchandise (origin, quality) and in any case Pierre would be riding on the reputation and investment of these brands (Bellure). Disney characters are also protected by copyright as original artistic works. Drop-shipping does not change anything: Pierre is the seller.
Conclusion
No, he cannot do it legally as such: he risks an infringement action (and the goods being seized). To do it legally he must obtain the owners' authorisation, i.e. a licence (paying royalties), or sell genuine officially licensed products bought from authorised suppliers.
Infringement actions, licences and the resale of genuine goods are taught after slide 200. This answer only uses what is needed for the exercise.

PRACTICE.title: TERRA-LOC, construction machinery
PRACTICE.facts:
TERRA-LOC SAS, a family company near Lille, sells and rents construction machinery (mini-excavators, loaders, dumpers) and does light maintenance. It operates a shop called "Terra-Loc Nord" and the website terraloc.fr. The manager wants to register as trademarks:
  1. the word "TERRA-LOC";
  2. the words "Mini Excavator" for mini-excavators;
  3. the yellow colour of all its machines;
  4. the reversing beep its machines make;
  5. the slogan "Built for the North";
  6. the shape of its bucket teeth, designed to dig better.
A garden-furniture shop in Lyon then opens a website called terra-loc.com.
tasks: Advise on the validity of each sign as a trademark (absolute grounds) and how to represent it.
Distinguish TERRA-LOC's company name, commercial name, domain name and trademark.
Can TERRA-LOC act against the Lyon shop, and on what basis?
hints: Invented words are the strongest; generic words, common colours and functional sounds or shapes are the weakest.
For the Lyon shop: different activity and a different area. What conditions apply to domain names and commercial names, and what action?
PRACTICE.model:
Issue
(1) Which signs can TERRA-LOC validly register? (2) Can it stop the Lyon shop's domain name?
Rule
Art. 3 Directive 2015/2436 (distinctive + capable of representation); Art. 4 Directive (devoid, descriptive, customary); acquired distinctiveness; shape exclusions; Vorsprung durch Technik (slogans). Other distinctive signs: protection through tort / unfair competition, against an identical/similar sign for an identical/similar activity in the same area, likely to cause confusion; principle of specialty.
Application

1. TERRA-LOC: invented word, not descriptive of machinery as such ("loc" evokes location/rental but the whole is fanciful). Distinctive. File as a word mark. Strongest sign.

2. "Mini Excavator" for mini-excavators: designates the goods. Generic, refused. Like "Shoes" for shoes.

3. Yellow: colour mark (sample + colour code, Libertel). Yellow is very common for construction machinery, so devoid of distinctive character; only acquired distinctiveness after long, exclusive use with surveys could save it, which is unrealistic here.

4. Reversing beep: sound mark (audio file or notation, Shield Mark). Representable, but the beep is a common, functional safety signal in the sector: consumers do not perceive it as an indication of origin. Not distinctive.

5. "Built for the North": a slogan can be a mark if it indicates origin (Vorsprung durch Technik). It refers to the geographical market and is promotional, so distinctiveness is arguable; a weak but possible mark, stronger if combined with TERRA-LOC.

6. Bucket teeth shape: designed to dig better, so necessary to obtain a technical result (like Lego). Excluded; acquired distinctiveness cannot cure it. Protection route: a patent if new and inventive, not a trademark.

Signs: TERRA-LOC SAS = registered company name; "Terra-Loc Nord" = commercial name; terraloc.fr = domain name; TERRA-LOC once registered = trademark.

Lyon shop: TERRA-LOC has only a domain name and commercial name for now, so no infringement action; the route is tort / unfair competition. Conditions are not met: the activity (garden furniture) is not similar, and the shop is in a different geographical area; confusion is unlikely. Principle of specialty.

Conclusion
Register TERRA-LOC as a word mark now (possibly with the slogan); drop "Mini Excavator", the yellow and the beep; consider a patent for the teeth. No realistic action against the Lyon shop. Business risk: without a registered mark, TERRA-LOC's name is only protected locally through tort.

PRACTICE.title: Noisette & Co chocolates
PRACTICE.facts:
Noisette & Co, a French chocolate start-up making all its products in Lyon, wants to register:
  1. "Belgian Chocolate Masters" for its chocolates;
  2. a logo including the Belgian national flag;
  3. the smell of roasted hazelnuts diffused in its shops;
  4. the shape of a hazelnut for its pralines, which is the main reason customers buy them;
  5. a short jingle played in its adverts, with an animation of a hazelnut rolling (image + sound);
  6. a repeated pattern of small brown hazelnuts on its packaging.
tasks: Identify the type of each sign and how it must be represented.
Identify every absolute ground for refusal.
Recommend the best protection strategy.
hints: One sign lies about geographical origin, one needs an authority's consent, one cannot be represented.
For the hazelnut shape, which of the three shape exclusions applies? For the jingle animation, which type of mark combines image and sound?
PRACTICE.model:
Issue
Which of these signs pass the absolute grounds, and how should they be filed?
Rule
Representation (Sieckmann; strawberries T-305/04); distinctiveness (Art. 4 Directive); shape exclusions; deceptive signs; flags and state emblems (consent of the competent authority).
Application

1. "Belgian Chocolate Masters" (word mark): the chocolates are made in Lyon, so the sign misleads on geographical origin: deceptive, refused. Even for Belgian chocolate it would be descriptive.

2. Logo with the Belgian flag (figurative mark): includes a state flag, refused unless the competent authority consents; it also reinforces the deceptive message.

3. Smell of roasted hazelnuts (olfactory mark): cannot be represented clearly and precisely with generally available technology (Sieckmann; ripe strawberries T-305/04). Refused.

4. Hazelnut shape (shape mark: graphic or photo reproduction): the shape is the main reason customers buy, so it gives substantial value to the goods; excluded, and acquired distinctiveness cannot cure it. Better route: a design (novelty + individual character, up to 25 years).

5. Jingle with rolling hazelnut = multimedia mark (image + sound), filed as an audiovisual file. Likely distinctive if original.

6. Hazelnut pattern = pattern mark: file a reproduction showing the repetition (description allowed). Hazelnuts on chocolate packaging evoke the ingredient, so distinctiveness is weak unless the design is original.

Conclusion
Register an invented word mark (e.g. a coined name) plus the multimedia jingle; protect the praline shape as a design; drop the Belgian references (deception and flag) and the smell. Business consequence: a refused or invalid mark means money spent on branding without exclusivity.

PRACTICE.title: Functions in practice
PRACTICE.facts: A website buys the keyword "Lacoste" on a search engine to show ads for cheap polo shirts of its own brand. Separately, a perfume maker sells "Chanel Lux N°5" in a bottle close to Chanel's. A market stall sells mugs bearing a football club's crest with a small sign "not official".
tasks: For each situation, which trademark function is at stake?
Cite the CJEU case that matches each situation and explain the principle.
hints: One is about keywords, one about free-riding on reputation, one about origin and disclaimers.
Google France; Bellure; Arsenal (and Hoffmann-La Roche for the origin definition).
PRACTICE.model:
Issue
Which functions of the trademark are harmed in each situation?
Rule
The CJEU protects four functions: origin, quality, communication/advertising, investment. Use of a sign is prohibited when it harms one of them.
Application

Keyword "Lacoste": advertising function; Google France (C-236/08 to C-238/08): use harming the mark as a promotional tool is prohibited (and origin is at risk if the ad does not make clear the polos are not Lacoste's).

"Chanel Lux N°5": reputation and investment functions; Bellure (C-487/07): taking unfair advantage of a famous mark's reputation is prohibited even without confusion.

Club crest mugs: origin function; Hoffmann-La Roche defines it; Arsenal (C-206/01): the slides teach that origin is not the only function, so a "not official" sign does not automatically make the use lawful.

Conclusion
All three uses are risky for the user; the owners can rely on the corresponding function. Business advice to the sellers: do not use third-party marks without a licence.
